HR@10 with one positive and 99 unique negatives measures ranking within a 100-item candidate set. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse recommender rankings relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation. Fixed candidates make comparisons reproducible but do not remove this bias. Preserve the pinned evaluator; describe gains specifically as sampled-candidate validation gains, without claiming full-catalog improvements. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Recommended uncertainty analysis: retain each model’s binary hit outcome for every validation user. For each of 10,000 bootstrap replicates, resample 200 users with replacement separately within each of the four datasets, using identical sampled user indices for both models. Compute each dataset’s mean hit difference, then average the four differences equally; report the observed macro difference, its 95% percentile interval, and category differences. This applies the paired-resampling principle documented by [SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html). The interval is conditional on the trained models, fixed candidates and represented datasets; it excludes training-seed variation, candidate-resampling uncertainty and generalization to new datasets.

Repeated checkpoint and architecture selection on the same validation users can overfit the selection criterion and inflate the winning score. Ordinary bootstrap intervals calculated after selecting the winner do not correct that adaptive selection bias. Predeclare checkpoint frequency, stopping rules and comparison criteria; record all attempted configurations and treat validation intervals as descriptive search diagnostics. Preserve the independent host-held test evaluation for final assessment. These recommendations follow [Cawley and Talbot’s analysis of model-selection bias](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).
